cards.title: Starting the Chapter-Specific Guidelines: Chapter 1
cards.content:
Up to now you have studied **general** guidelines that apply everywhere. This lesson begins **Section I.C, Chapter-Specific Coding Guidelines** — rules for particular diagnoses and conditions.

We start with **Chapter 1: Certain Infectious and Parasitic Diseases (A00-B99), U07.1, U09.9**, and three of its guidelines:

• **I.C.1.a — HIV infections.** When to assign **B20** (HIV disease), **Z21** (asymptomatic HIV infection status), or **R75** (inconclusive laboratory evidence of HIV); how to sequence them; and how to code pregnancy, HIV testing, antiretroviral therapy, and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP).
• **I.C.1.b — Infectious agents** as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters (categories **B95**, **B96**, **B97**).
• **I.C.1.c — Infections resistant to antibiotics** (category **Z16**).

HIV coding is a frequent exam topic because it is one of the few places where the guidelines override the usual inpatient rule for uncertain diagnoses.

boxes.b: B95, B96, B97 as added codes

cards.title: In Plain English: How Chapter-Specific Guidelines Fit In
cards.content:
Section I.C introduces the chapter-specific guidelines. It makes three points:

• They apply **in addition to** the general coding guidelines — they do not replace them.
• **Unless otherwise indicated**, they apply to **all health care settings** (inpatient and outpatient).
• For **selecting the principal diagnosis**, refer to **Section II**.

**What it does NOT mean:** a chapter-specific guideline does not automatically apply only to inpatients. Watch for any guideline that "otherwise indicates" a setting; if none is stated, it applies everywhere.

cards.question: According to Section I.C, to which settings do the chapter-specific guidelines apply?
options: Only hospital inpatient admissions
Only outpatient encounters
All health care settings, unless otherwise indicated
Only the settings named in Section II
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C states, "Unless otherwise indicated, these guidelines apply to all health care settings." Options A and B limit them to one setting, which the guideline does not do. Option D is wrong because Section II is referenced only for guidelines on the selection of principal diagnosis.

visual.hint: Read the second sentence of Section I.C.

cards.title: HIV Rule 1: Code Only Confirmed Cases
cards.content:
Section I.C.1.a.1 says: **code only confirmed cases** of HIV infection/illness.

**Why this is special:** it is an **exception to the hospital inpatient guideline in Section II, H**. Normally, Section II.H lets inpatient coders code a condition documented as "probable," "suspected," "likely," and similar terms as if it existed. That does **not** apply to HIV.

**What counts as confirmation?**

• Confirmation does **not** require documentation of **positive serology or culture** for HIV.
• The **provider's diagnostic statement** that the patient is **HIV positive** or has an **HIV-related illness** is sufficient.

**Exam trap:** "Suspected HIV" on an inpatient discharge summary is **not** coded as HIV, even though other suspected conditions might be coded as if established for an inpatient.

boxes.b: Provider statement of HIV+ or HIV illness

cards.question: An inpatient discharge summary lists "suspected HIV infection." No HIV-positive status or HIV-related illness is documented. What does Section I.C.1.a.1 instruct?
options: Code only confirmed cases of HIV; this suspected HIV is not coded as HIV
Code HIV as if it were established, as for any inpatient uncertain diagnosis
Code HIV only if positive serology is in the record
Code B20 because the patient is an inpatient
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.1 says to code only confirmed cases of HIV infection/illness, and that this is an exception to the hospital inpatient guideline Section II, H. Option B applies the general inpatient rule, which HIV is an exception to. Option C is wrong because confirmation does not require positive serology or culture; the provider's diagnostic statement is sufficient. Option D is wrong because B20 requires confirmed HIV disease, not just an inpatient setting.

visual.hint: HIV is an exception to which inpatient rule?

cards.title: HIV Rule 2: When to Assign B20
cards.content:
Section I.C.1.a.2(a) says **B20, Human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] disease**, should be assigned if:

• the term **"AIDS"** is documented, or
• the term **"HIV disease"** is documented, or
• the patient is **treated for any HIV-related illness**, or
• the patient is described as having **any condition(s) resulting from HIV positive status**.

**Once B20, always B20 (I.C.1.a.2(g)):**

• Patients with a **prior diagnosis of an HIV-related illness** are coded to **B20**.
• Once an HIV-related illness has developed, **B20 should always be assigned on every subsequent admission/encounter**.
• A patient previously diagnosed with any HIV illness (B20) should **never** be assigned **R75** or **Z21**.

boxes.b: Always B20; never R75 or Z21 later

cards.title: HIV Rule 3: Sequencing B20
cards.content:
Sections I.C.1.a.2(b) through (d) explain where B20 goes.

**(b) Admitted for an HIV-related condition:**
• Principal diagnosis: **B20**, followed by codes for all reported HIV-related conditions.
• **Exception:** if the reason for admission is **hemolytic-uremic syndrome associated with HIV disease**, assign **D59.31, Infection-associated hemolytic-uremic syndrome**, followed by **B20**.

**(c) HIV disease, admitted for an unrelated condition** (such as a traumatic injury):
• Principal diagnosis: the **unrelated condition** (e.g., the nature of injury code).
• **B20** is a **secondary** diagnosis, along with codes for other documented conditions.

**(d) Newly diagnosed or not:**
• Whether the patient is **newly diagnosed** or has had **previous admissions/encounters** for HIV is **irrelevant** to sequencing.

cards.title: Worked Example: Same Patient, Two Admissions
cards.content:
**Admission 1:** A patient with AIDS is admitted for treatment of an HIV-related illness.

• **Guideline:** I.C.1.a.2(b).
• **Decision:** **B20** is the principal diagnosis, followed by the code(s) for the HIV-related condition(s).

**Admission 2:** The same patient is later admitted for a traumatic injury from a fall. The injury is unrelated to HIV.

• **Guideline:** I.C.1.a.2(c).
• **Decision:** The **injury** (nature of injury code) is the principal diagnosis. **B20** is a secondary diagnosis. Other documented conditions are also coded as secondary diagnoses.
• Under I.C.1.a.2(g), **B20** is still assigned — once an HIV-related illness has developed, B20 is assigned on every subsequent encounter.

**Exception to remember:** if the admission were for **hemolytic-uremic syndrome associated with HIV disease**, **D59.31** would be sequenced before **B20**.

cards.question: A patient with HIV disease is admitted for treatment of a fractured femur from a car accident. The fracture is unrelated to HIV. What is the correct sequencing under Section I.C.1.a.2(c)?
options: B20 as principal diagnosis, fracture as secondary
Fracture only; B20 is not reported for unrelated admissions
Z21 as principal diagnosis
The fracture (nature of injury code) as principal diagnosis, B20 as secondary
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(c) states that if a patient with HIV disease is admitted for an unrelated condition (such as a traumatic injury), the code for the unrelated condition should be the principal diagnosis and B20 is reported as a secondary diagnosis. Option A applies only when admitted for an HIV-related condition. Option C is wrong because a patient with HIV disease is coded to B20, not Z21. Option B is wrong because B20 is still reported, as a secondary diagnosis.

cards.question: A patient is admitted because of hemolytic-uremic syndrome associated with HIV disease. According to Section I.C.1.a.2(b), how is this sequenced?
options: B20, followed by D59.31
D59.31, Infection-associated hemolytic-uremic syndrome, followed by B20
D59.31 only
Z21, followed by D59.31
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(b) gives this as the exception to the B20-first rule: assign code D59.31, Infection-associated hemolytic-uremic syndrome, followed by code B20. Option A follows the general rule, which does not apply to this exception. Option C leaves out B20. Option D is wrong because the patient has HIV disease, which is coded to B20, not Z21.

visual.hint: This is the one named exception to B20 first.

cards.question: A patient is newly diagnosed with HIV disease during an admission for an HIV-related illness. Does the new diagnosis change the sequencing?
options: Yes; newly diagnosed patients are coded with Z21 first
Yes; the HIV-related illness is sequenced before B20 for new diagnoses
No; whether the patient is newly diagnosed is irrelevant to sequencing, so B20 is principal followed by the HIV-related condition
No; B20 is never principal
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(d) says whether the patient is newly diagnosed or has had previous admissions/encounters for HIV conditions is irrelevant to the sequencing decision, and I.C.1.a.2(b) says that for admission for an HIV-related condition, B20 is principal followed by the HIV-related conditions. Options A and B invent a different rule for new diagnoses. Option D contradicts I.C.1.a.2(b).

visual.hint: Does timing of the diagnosis matter?

cards.title: HIV Rule 4: Z21 and R75
cards.content:
Two codes are for patients **without** HIV disease as described for B20.

**Z21, Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status** — I.C.1.a.2(e):
• Assign when **"HIV positive," "HIV test positive,"** or similar terminology is documented, **and** there is **no documentation of symptoms or HIV-related illness**.

**R75, Inconclusive laboratory evidence of human immunodeficiency virus [HIV]** — I.C.1.a.2(f):
• Patients with documentation of **inconclusive HIV serology** may be assigned R75.

**The one-way door — I.C.1.a.2(g):**
• Patients previously diagnosed with **any HIV illness (B20)** should **never** be assigned **R75** or **Z21**.

**Exam trap:** "HIV positive" alone is **Z21**, not B20. But once the patient has had an HIV-related illness, it is **B20** from then on, even if the patient feels well today.

boxes.b: AIDS, HIV disease, or HIV-related illness
HIV positive, no symptoms or HIV illness

cards.question: The provider documents "HIV positive." There is no documentation of symptoms or any HIV-related illness, now or in the past. Which code does Section I.C.1.a.2(e) direct?
options: Z21, Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status
B20, Human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] disease
R75, Inconclusive laboratory evidence of human immunodeficiency virus [HIV]
Z11.4, Encounter for screening for human immunodeficiency virus [HIV]
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(e) states that when "HIV positive," "HIV test positive," or similar terminology is documented, and there is no documentation of symptoms or HIV-related illness, code Z21 should be assigned. Option B requires AIDS, HIV disease, or an HIV-related illness. Option C is for inconclusive serology, not a positive status. Option D is for screening a patient without signs or symptoms, not for documented HIV-positive status.

visual.hint: Are there symptoms or an HIV-related illness?

cards.question: A patient had an HIV-related illness two years ago. Today the patient is seen and the provider documents "HIV positive, currently no symptoms." Which code is correct under Section I.C.1.a.2(g)?
options: Z21, because the patient has no symptoms today
R75, because current status is unclear
No HIV code, because there are no symptoms
B20, because once an HIV-related illness has developed, B20 is assigned on every subsequent encounter
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(g) states that patients with documentation of a prior diagnosis of an HIV-related illness should be coded to B20, that B20 should always be assigned on every subsequent admission/encounter once an HIV-related illness has developed, and that such patients should never be assigned R75 or Z21. Options A and B assign codes the guideline says never to use for these patients. Option C ignores the guideline.

visual.hint: Once a patient has had an HIV-related illness, can the code change back?

cards.title: HIV Rule 5: Pregnancy, Childbirth and the Puerperium
cards.content:
Section I.C.1.a.2(h) covers HIV during **pregnancy, childbirth or the puerperium** (the period after delivery).

**Symptomatic HIV disease or an HIV-related illness:**
1. A code from subcategory **O98.7**, Human immunodeficiency [HIV] disease complicating pregnancy, childbirth and the puerperium
2. **B20**
3. Additional code(s) for any HIV-related illness(es)

**Asymptomatic HIV infection status, or HIV-positive:**
1. A code from subcategory **O98.7**
2. **Z21**

**Why O98.7 comes first:** the guideline states that **codes from Chapter 15 always take sequencing priority**.

boxes.b: O98.7, then B20, then illness codes

cards.question: A pregnant patient is documented as HIV positive with no symptoms and no HIV-related illness. According to Section I.C.1.a.2(h), how is this coded?
options: Z21 only
A code from subcategory O98.7, followed by Z21
B20, followed by a code from O98.7
A code from subcategory O98.7, followed by B20
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(h) states that when a patient presents during pregnancy, childbirth or the puerperium with documented asymptomatic HIV infection status or is HIV-positive, assign a code from subcategory O98.7 followed by code Z21. Option A leaves out O98.7, and Chapter 15 codes always take sequencing priority. Options C and D use B20, which is for symptomatic HIV disease or an HIV-related illness (and option C also puts O98.7 second).

visual.hint: Is the patient symptomatic, and which chapter goes first?

cards.title: HIV Rule 6: Encounters for HIV Testing
cards.content:
Section I.C.1.a.2(i) depends on whether the patient has **signs or symptoms**.

**No signs or symptoms, tested for HIV:**
• Assign **Z11.4, Encounter for screening for human immunodeficiency virus [HIV]**.
• Use additional codes for any associated **high-risk behavior**, if applicable.

**Signs or symptoms present, tested for HIV:**
• **Code the signs and symptoms.**
• **Z71.7, Human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] counseling**, may be added if counseling is provided during the encounter for the test.
• **Do not** assign Z11.4 when HIV signs or symptoms are present.

**Follow-up visit for test results:**
• **Negative** result: assign **Z71.7**.
• **Positive** result: follow the earlier HIV guidelines and assign codes as appropriate.

boxes.b: Code them; Z71.7 if counseled; no Z11.4

cards.title: Worked Example: Three Testing Visits
cards.content:
**Visit A:** A patient with no signs or symptoms asks for an HIV test. The provider documents a high-risk behavior.
• **Decision:** **Z11.4**, plus an additional code for the associated high-risk behavior (I.C.1.a.2(i)).

**Visit B:** A patient with signs and symptoms that the provider thinks could be HIV-related is tested, and the provider counsels the patient.
• **Decision:** Code the **signs and symptoms**. **Z71.7** may be added because counseling was provided. **Z11.4 is not assigned** because signs or symptoms are present.

**Visit C:** Visit A's patient returns for results. The result is **negative**.
• **Decision:** **Z71.7, Human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] counseling.**

**Exam trap:** Z11.4 is a **screening** code — it is for patients **without** signs or symptoms.

cards.question: A patient with signs and symptoms of HIV presents for HIV testing, and counseling is provided. Which coding approach follows Section I.C.1.a.2(i)?
options: Z11.4 only
Z11.4 followed by the signs and symptoms
Code the signs and symptoms; Z71.7 may be added for the counseling; do not assign Z11.4
B20, because the patient has symptoms
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(i) says that if a patient with signs or symptoms presents for HIV testing, code the signs and symptoms; Z71.7 may be assigned if counseling is provided; and Z11.4 should not be assigned if HIV signs or symptoms are present. Options A and B use Z11.4, which is not allowed when signs or symptoms are present. Option D is wrong because only confirmed cases of HIV are coded (I.C.1.a.1); a test visit with symptoms is not a confirmed diagnosis.

cards.question: A patient returns to learn the results of an HIV test, and the result is negative. Which code does Section I.C.1.a.2(i) direct?
options: Z71.7, Human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] counseling
R75, Inconclusive laboratory evidence of human immunodeficiency virus [HIV]
Z11.4, Encounter for screening for human immunodeficiency virus [HIV]
Z21, Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(i) states that when a patient presents for follow up regarding HIV test results and the result is negative, assign code Z71.7. Option C is for the testing (screening) encounter, not the results follow-up. Option B is for inconclusive serology, not a negative result. Option D is for a documented HIV-positive status.

visual.hint: What does the guideline say for a negative result?

cards.title: HIV Rule 7: Antiretroviral Medication
cards.content:
Section I.C.1.a.2(j) covers patients **currently managed on antiretroviral medications**.

• **Documented HIV disease, HIV-related illness or AIDS** and on antiretroviral medication: assign **B20**.
• **Documented HIV positive status** and on antiretroviral medication: assign **Z21**, **in the absence of** any additional documentation of HIV disease, HIV-related illness or AIDS.
• **Z79.899, Other long term (current) drug therapy**, **may** be assigned as an additional code to identify the long-term (current) use of antiretroviral medications.

**What it does NOT mean:** being on antiretroviral medication does **not** by itself turn HIV positive status into B20. The choice still depends on what is documented.

cards.question: A patient documented as HIV positive is managed on antiretroviral medication. There is no documentation of HIV disease, HIV-related illness or AIDS. What does Section I.C.1.a.2(j) direct?
options: B20, because the patient takes antiretroviral medication
Z79.899 only
Z21, with Z79.899 permitted as an additional code
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(j) states that a patient with documented HIV positive status currently managed on antiretroviral medication is assigned Z21 in the absence of additional documentation of HIV disease, HIV-related illness or AIDS, and that Z79.899 may be assigned as an additional code for the long-term use of antiretroviral medications. Option A wrongly treats the medication as proof of HIV disease. Option C is for inconclusive serology. Option B leaves out the HIV status code; Z79.899 is an additional code.

visual.hint: What does the documentation say about HIV disease?

cards.title: HIV Rule 8: Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)
cards.content:
Section I.C.1.a.2(k) covers encounters for **HIV prophylaxis**.

• When a patient presents for administration of **pre-exposure prophylaxis** medication for HIV, assign **Z29.81, Encounter for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis**.
• **PrEP** is intended to **prevent infection** in people who are at risk for getting HIV through sex or injection drug use.
• **Any risk factors** for HIV should **also be coded**.

**Exam trap — PrEP vs antiretroviral management:** PrEP is for someone **without** HIV who is trying to prevent infection (Z29.81). Antiretroviral management under (j) is for a patient who already has documented HIV disease (B20) or HIV positive status (Z21).

cards.question: A patient presents for administration of HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis medication. Which statement follows Section I.C.1.a.2(k)?
options: Assign Z21 because the patient is taking HIV medication
Assign Z29.81, Encounter for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis, and also code any risk factors for HIV
Assign Z11.4 because the visit relates to HIV
Assign Z79.899 only
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(k) states that when a patient presents for administration of pre-exposure prophylaxis medication for HIV, assign code Z29.81, and any risk factors for HIV should also be coded. Option A is for documented HIV positive status, which PrEP patients do not have. Option C is for screening tests, not PrEP administration. Option D is an optional add-on for antiretroviral management in patients with HIV under I.C.1.a.2(j), not the PrEP code.

visual.hint: What is PrEP intended to do?

cards.title: In Plain English: Adding the Organism Code
cards.content:
Some infections are classified in **chapters other than Chapter 1**, and their codes **do not identify the organism**. Section I.C.1.b says that in these cases you need an **additional code from Chapter 1** to identify the organism.

The categories to use:

• **B95** — Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and Enterococcus as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
• **B96** — Other bacterial agents as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
• **B97** — Viral agents as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters

**How you know:** an **instructional note** at the infection code advises that an additional organism code is required.

**What it does NOT mean:** B95-B97 are **additional** codes. They identify the organism; they do not replace the code for the infection.

boxes.b: Instructional note at the infection code

cards.title: Worked Example: Infection Code Without an Organism
cards.content:
**Documentation:** A patient is treated for an infection that is classified in a body-system chapter (not Chapter 1). The provider documents that the infection is caused by a Staphylococcus organism. The infection code itself does not name any organism, and the Tabular List has an instructional note saying to use an additional code to identify the organism.

**Which guideline applies?** Section I.C.1.b.

**Decision:**

• Assign the code for the **infection**.
• Add a code from category **B95** (Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and Enterococcus as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters) to identify the organism.

**If the organism were a virus,** the additional code would come from **B97**; for other bacterial agents, **B96**.

cards.question: An infection classified to a chapter other than Chapter 1 has a code that does not identify the organism. The documented organism is a virus. According to Section I.C.1.b, what should be added?
options: A code from category B95
A code from category B96
A code from category B97
Nothing; the infection code is sufficient
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.b states that a code from category B97, Viral agents as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters, is used as an additional code to identify the organism. Option A (B95) is for Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and Enterococcus. Option B (B96) is for other bacterial agents. Option D is wrong because when no organism is identified in the infection code, an additional Chapter 1 code is necessary.

visual.hint: Match the organism type to B95, B96 or B97.

cards.title: In Plain English: Antibiotic-Resistant Infections
cards.content:
Section I.C.1.c says many bacterial infections are **resistant to current antibiotics**, and it is necessary to **identify all infections documented as antibiotic resistant**.

The rule:

• Assign a code from category **Z16, Resistance to antimicrobial drugs**,
• **following** the infection code,
• **only if** the infection code **does not** already identify drug resistance.

**What it does NOT mean:**
• Z16 is not placed **before** the infection code.
• Z16 is not added when the infection code **already** includes the drug resistance — that would repeat the same information.

boxes.b: Infection code does not show resistance

cards.question: A provider documents an infection as antibiotic resistant. The infection code already identifies the drug resistance. According to Section I.C.1.c, what should the coder do about category Z16?
options: Do not assign Z16, because the infection code already identifies the drug resistance
Assign Z16 after the infection code
Assign Z16 first, then the infection code
Assign Z16 only for inpatient encounters
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.c says to assign a code from category Z16 following the infection code only if the infection code does not identify drug resistance. Here it does, so Z16 is not added. Option C reverses the order and adds an unnecessary code. Option B would apply only if the infection code did not identify drug resistance. Option D is wrong because Section I.C says chapter-specific guidelines apply to all health care settings unless otherwise indicated, and I.C.1.c does not limit the setting.

visual.hint: Does the infection code already include the resistance?

cards.title: Applying Chapter 1 Rules on a Real Record
cards.content:
**For any record that mentions HIV:**

1. **Is HIV confirmed?** Only confirmed cases are coded. The provider's statement of HIV positive or HIV-related illness is enough; serology is not required (I.C.1.a.1).
2. **Pick the status code:**
   • AIDS, HIV disease, HIV-related illness, or any **prior** HIV-related illness: **B20** (a), (g)
   • HIV positive, no symptoms or HIV-related illness: **Z21** (e)
   • Inconclusive serology: **R75** (f) — never for a patient previously assigned B20
3. **Pregnancy, childbirth or puerperium?** O98.7 first, then B20 (plus HIV illnesses) or Z21 (h).
4. **Sequence:** admitted for an HIV-related condition = B20 first (except HIV-associated hemolytic-uremic syndrome: D59.31, then B20); admitted for an unrelated condition = that condition first, B20 secondary (b), (c).
5. **Testing visit?** No signs/symptoms: Z11.4. Signs/symptoms: code them (Z71.7 if counseled; no Z11.4). Negative results follow-up: Z71.7 (i).
6. **On antiretrovirals?** B20 or Z21 based on documentation; Z79.899 may be added (j). **PrEP?** Z29.81 plus risk factors (k).

**For infections from other chapters:**

7. Infection code lacks the organism? Add B95, B96 or B97 (I.C.1.b).
8. Documented antibiotic resistance not shown in the infection code? Add Z16 after the infection code (I.C.1.c).

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.content:
• Chapter-specific guidelines apply in **all settings unless otherwise indicated** (I.C).
• **Code only confirmed HIV** — an exception to the inpatient uncertain diagnosis rule (II.H). The provider's statement is enough; no serology needed (I.C.1.a.1).
• **B20** for AIDS, HIV disease, or any HIV-related illness. **Once B20, always B20** — never R75 or Z21 afterward (I.C.1.a.2(a), (g)).
• **Z21** for HIV positive with no symptoms or HIV-related illness; **R75** for inconclusive serology (e), (f).
• Admitted **for** an HIV-related condition: **B20 first** (exception: **D59.31** then B20). Admitted for an **unrelated** condition: that condition first, B20 secondary. New vs. old diagnosis does not matter (b)-(d).
• Pregnancy: **O98.7 first** — Chapter 15 always takes priority (h).
• Testing: **Z11.4** only without signs/symptoms; **Z71.7** for counseling or negative results (i). Antiretrovirals: B20 or Z21 per documentation, Z79.899 optional (j). PrEP: **Z29.81** plus risk factors (k).
• **B95-B97** identify organisms for infections coded elsewhere; **Z16** follows the infection code only when resistance is not already in it (I.C.1.b, I.C.1.c).

boxes.b: HIV is an exception to II.H
Disease or illness; once B20, always

cards.question: Under Section I.C.1.a.1, which of the following is sufficient to confirm HIV for coding purposes?
options: Only a positive HIV culture
Only positive HIV serology
A nurse's note that the patient may have HIV
The provider's diagnostic statement that the patient is HIV positive or has an HIV-related illness
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.1 states that confirmation does not require documentation of positive serology or culture for HIV; the provider's diagnostic statement that the patient is HIV positive or has an HIV-related illness is sufficient. Options A and B are wrong because serology or culture is not required. Option C is uncertain ("may have") and is not the provider's diagnostic statement; only confirmed cases are coded.

visual.hint: Whose statement confirms HIV, and does it require lab proof?

cards.question: A patient previously diagnosed with an HIV-related illness now has documentation of inconclusive HIV serology. Which code applies under Section I.C.1.a.2(g)?
options: R75, Inconclusive laboratory evidence of human immunodeficiency virus [HIV]
B20, Human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] disease
Z21, Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status
Z11.4, Encounter for screening for human immunodeficiency virus [HIV]
cards.explanation: Correct: Section I.C.1.a.2(g) states that patients with a prior diagnosis of an HIV-related illness should be coded to B20 and should never be assigned R75 or Z21. Options A and C are the two codes the guideline says never to assign for these patients. Option D is a screening code for patients without signs or symptoms being tested; it does not describe this patient's HIV status.

visual.hint: Which codes does (g) say are never assigned to these patients?
